sections.heading: How to generate a regex
sections.body:
Open the tool, describe what you want to match, and let it write the pattern. You do not need to know regex syntax. Plain words are enough, such as an email address or a date like 28/11/2026.

1. Open [Regex Generator](https://regex-generator.lazur.app/).
2. Type what you want to match in Describe the pattern.
3. Optional: paste text you have into Sample text to test on.
4. Run the tool. The answer comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.
5. Copy the regex with one click.

**The tool writes the pattern, but you still check it.** It is an AI tool, so the first answer can miss an edge case. The sample text box is there for that check.

sections.heading: What to write in the description
sections.body:
The better the description, the better the pattern. Say what the text looks like, how long it is, and which parts can change. Say what must not match, too.

- Name each part. Five digits, then an optional dash and four more digits, is clearer than a ZIP code.
- Give one example. Match years like 2026, not 26.
- Say what to ignore. Letters in any case, spaces at the start of a line, and so on.

If the first answer is too loose or too strict, add one sentence to the description that fixes it and run the tool again.

sections.heading: Test the regex before you use it
sections.body:
A regex can match more than you meant. Paste two kinds of lines into Sample text to test on: lines that should match and lines that should not. If the result misses one, or catches one it should skip, change the description and test again.

Keep the test short. Ten lines that cover the normal case and the odd cases tell you more than a long file that looks much the same. Once every line gives the right answer, copy the regex into your editor, search box or code.

Start with the text you want to find. One example is enough to begin, but describe the whole pattern, not only that example. If you describe only the example, the regex may match that line and nothing else.

1. Open the [regex generator from text](https://regex-generator.lazur.app/from-text).

3. Paste a few lines of text into Sample text to test on, including lines that should not match.

The answer comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds, so you can change the description and run it again without waiting long.

sections.heading: Describe the parts that change
sections.body:
Most bad regexes come from a description that skips the parts that vary. Compare these two:

- Too vague: a phone number.
- Clear: ten digits in a row, with an optional dash after the third and sixth digit.

Say how long the text is, which characters it may use, and whether it sits at the start or end of a line. A clear description usually gives a better regex on the first run.

**Name the part you want to keep.** If you only need the number inside a longer line, say that. The tool can then write a pattern that finds the number and skips the rest.

sections.heading: Test the result on text you already have
sections.body:
Paste lines from your own files into Sample text to test on. Include the lines you want to catch and the ones you want to skip. If a line is missed, add it to the description and run the tool again.

Short tests catch most problems. Keep the sample to a few dozen lines while you tune the pattern. When a long file gives the same answers as the short sample, you can trust the regex more.

Try the value in different places too. Put it at the start of a line, in the middle and at the end. A regex that fits one line can fail on the next, and this check finds that quickly.

faq.q: Is there an alternative to regex?
faq.a: Yes, for simple jobs. Plain string functions such as contains, starts with or split can find fixed text without a pattern. Use a regex when the text varies, such as digits, dates or several possible words. The tool on this page writes regular expressions, so it helps when you need the pattern.

Yes. Regex is built into most programming languages, text editors, search tools and log viewers. It is still the standard way to describe a flexible text pattern. Learning the basics helps you read the patterns that other people and tools write.

faq.q: How to use regex on a string?
faq.a: Put the regex into your code's matching function, then test it on a few strings. In JavaScript you can call the test method on a regular expression, and in Python you can use re.search. Copy the regex from this tool, then check it against lines that should match and lines that should not.

faq.q: Where can I generate regex patterns online?
faq.a: There are several online tools for regex. This one writes a pattern from a plain-English description and optional sample text. Check its output on your own examples, because an AI tool can miss an edge case.

sections.heading: Get a regex for your Python code
sections.body:
Start with the text you want Python to find. Describe it in plain words, the way you would explain it to a coworker. You do not need regex syntax to start.

1. Open the [regex generator for Python](https://regex-generator.lazur.app/python).
2. Type the pattern in Describe the pattern, for example: a line that starts with a date like 2026-11-28.
3. Paste a few lines from your data into Sample text to test on.
4. Run the tool and copy the regex it gives you.

You can mention Python in the description, but the tool does not say which regex syntax it writes. Treat the output as a draft until you have tested it in Python.

sections.heading: Test the regex with re
sections.body:
Python's built-in re module does the matching. Two functions cover most jobs.

- re.search looks through the whole text and returns the first match, or None if nothing matches.
- re.findall returns every match as a list of strings.

Try both on your sample lines. If re.search returns None on a line that should match, the pattern is too strict. If it matches a line that should not, the pattern is too loose. Fix the description or the regex, then test again.

The regular expression section of the Python re documentation lists every special character. Use it as the reference when you check a symbol you do not recognize.

sections.heading: Write the pattern as a raw string
sections.body:
In Python, put an r in front of the quotes around the pattern, which makes it a raw string. A raw string keeps backslashes as they are, so the regex gets exactly the characters the tool wrote.

**Without the r, Python reads some backslash pairs as special characters.** For example, a backslash followed by n becomes a new line. That mistake gives a pattern that looks right on the page but matches the wrong text.

sections.heading: Reuse the pattern and check edge cases
sections.body:
If your code runs the same pattern many times, compile it once with re.compile and then call search on the result. Python also keeps recent patterns in a cache, so this helps most in large loops.

Check edge cases too: empty lines, extra spaces and upper case letters. If you need case-insensitive matching, the re documentation shows the flag to use.

Python quantifiers such as star and plus are greedy by default. They take as much text as they can, so test with a long line as well as a short one.

sections.heading: If you code by voice
sections.body: If you dictate notes or code comments on a Mac all day, Lazur works in any app. Hold two keys and talk, and it types for you.

faq.a: Yes, by default. Quantifiers such as star and plus match as much text as they can while the whole pattern still fits. Add a question mark after the quantifier to make it lazy, so it matches as little as possible. Test with a long line to see which one you get.

faq.q: Is there a cheat sheet for Python regex?
faq.a: The regular expression syntax section of the official Python re documentation lists every special character and what it does. That section works as a cheat sheet. When you are unsure about a symbol in the regex this tool writes, compare it with that list.

pages.description: Write a regex for Discord AutoMod from a plain-English description, then check it fits Discord's Rust syntax and 260 character limit. Free to try.
pages.claim: Discord's developer docs allow up to 10 regex patterns per AutoMod rule, each 260 characters or less, in Rust syntax. This tool writes a regex from your description but does not promise Rust syntax, so check it first. Free.

sections.heading: What Discord accepts for regex
sections.body:
Discord's developer documentation for AutoMod keyword rules sets the regex limits. A rule can have up to 10 regex patterns, and each pattern must be 260 characters or less. The docs say only Rust flavored regex is supported at the moment.

A wildcard is simpler when it is enough. An asterisk at the start or end of a keyword matches more forms of the word. Keywords are not case sensitive, and each keyword can be up to 60 characters. Use a regex only when a wildcard cannot describe the text you want to catch.

Limits can change, so check the current numbers in your server's AutoMod settings before you save a rule.

sections.heading: Describe the message pattern
sections.body:
Describe what the message looks like, not only one word. For example: an invite link to discord.gg followed by letters or digits. Name the parts that can change, and say what the rest of the message may contain.

1. Open the [regex generator for Discord](https://regex-generator.lazur.app/discord).
2. Type the message pattern in Describe the pattern.
3. Paste sample messages into Sample text to test on, including messages that should be allowed.
4. Run the tool and copy the regex.

Keep the finished regex under 260 characters. A long description can produce a long regex, so shorten the description if the result is too big. Count the characters in the copied regex, not in your description, because the limit applies to the pattern itself.

sections.heading: Check it fits Rust syntax
sections.body:
The tool does not promise a flavor, so check the pattern against Rust syntax before you save it. JavaScript and Python are different. A pattern that passes a Python test can still fail in Discord, or match a different set of messages.

Use a Rust regex tester to run the pattern on your samples. Discord's developer documentation suggests Rustexp for this. Run the samples again after every change, even a small one.

sections.heading: Test with real messages and keep it small
sections.body:
Test against real messages from your server, not only made-up examples. Keep a list of messages that must be allowed and messages that must be caught. Add a regex only when a wildcard keyword is not enough.

A rule can hold up to 10 patterns, so combine the cases you need into a few clear patterns instead of many small ones. A short pattern is easier to read later when someone asks why a message was removed.

Try messages with extra spaces, links, emoji and line breaks. Real chat rarely looks like the example you started with. Write down what each pattern is for next to the rule, so you can change it later without guessing.

faq.a: Yes. Discord's developer documentation for AutoMod keyword rules includes regex patterns. Each rule can have up to 10 patterns, and each pattern can be 260 characters or less. Discord currently supports only Rust flavored regex, so check your pattern against Rust syntax.

faq.q: Is a wildcard simpler than regex on Discord?
faq.a: Often, yes. An asterisk at the start or end of a keyword matches word endings and beginnings. Keywords are not case sensitive, and each keyword can be up to 60 characters. Use a regex only when a wildcard cannot describe the pattern you need.

faq.q: What regex flavor does Discord use?
faq.a: Discord's developer documentation says only Rust flavored regex is supported at the moment. Patterns written for other flavors can behave differently, so test your regex in a Rust tester before you rely on it in a server.
